eras/awakenings-missions/summary: Evangelical revivals swept Britain and North America through the preaching of Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield and John and Charles Wesley, giving birth to Methodism and a transatlantic evangelical identity centred on conversion, the cross, the Bible and activism. The Moravians pioneered Protestant world mission, followed by William Carey and new missionary societies. Evangelicals led campaigns against the slave trade, abolished in Britain in 1807. The French Revolution shook European Catholicism, the Second Great Awakening spawned new American denominations and restorationist movements, and Adventist expectation peaked in 1844.
eras/awakenings-missions/globalNotes/0/t: Freed Black Loyalists founded Freetown, Sierra Leone (1792), with Methodist and Baptist congregations; the Church Missionary Society's Fourah Bay College (1827) educated Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a rescued Yoruba slave.
eras/awakenings-missions/globalNotes/1/t: African Americans formed independent churches, notably Richard Allen's African Methodist Episcopal Church (1816), while slave Christianity developed its own spirituals and 'invisible institution'.
eras/awakenings-missions/globalNotes/2/t: Korean scholars, studying Catholic books from China, formed a lay-led church (1784) without missionaries; persecutions killed thousands, including in 1801 and 1839. Robert Morrison, the first Protestant missionary to China, arrived in 1807.
eras/awakenings-missions/globalNotes/3/t: London Missionary Society workers reached Tahiti (1797); King Pōmare II's conversion (1812) began Polynesian Christianity, often spread thereafter by Pacific Islander missionaries themselves.
eras/awakenings-missions/globalNotes/4/t: William Carey and the Serampore mission (from 1800) translated Scripture into dozens of Indian languages; the East India Company's ban on missionaries was lifted in 1813.
eras/awakenings-missions/globalNotes/5/t: Paisius Velichkovsky's Slavonic Philokalia (1793) and the elder Seraphim of Sarov (d. 1833) sparked a hesychast revival; Russian Orthodox missionaries reached Alaska (1794).
eras/awakenings-missions/globalNotes/6/t: Independence wars (1810–1825) disrupted the colonial church; many bishops were royalist, while priests such as Miguel Hidalgo and José María Morelos led insurgencies in Mexico.
eras/modern-era/summary: Industrialisation, Darwinism and historical criticism of the Bible challenged traditional faith, producing liberal theology, Catholic ultramontanism (papal infallibility, 1870) and Protestant fundamentalism. The 'Great Century' of missions planted churches across Africa, Asia and the Pacific, often entangled with colonialism yet increasingly led by local Christians. The Holiness movement and the Azusa Street Revival (1906) launched Pentecostalism, destined to become one of the fastest-growing forms of Christianity. The world wars, totalitarian persecution in the Soviet Union and the Confessing Church's resistance to Nazism tested the churches profoundly, while the Edinburgh Conference (1910) began the modern ecumenical movement.
eras/modern-era/keyThemes/3: Holiness and the birth of Pentecostalism
eras/modern-era/globalNotes/0/text: Samuel Ajayi Crowther became the first African Anglican bishop (1864); prophets such as William Wadé Harris (Ivory Coast, 1913–1915) and Simon Kimbangu (Congo, 1921) led mass movements, and African Initiated Churches like the Zionist and Aladura churches multiplied.
eras/modern-era/globalNotes/1/text: The Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), led by a visionary influenced by Protestant tracts, devastated China; after the Boxer Uprising (1900) Chinese Christians built self-governing churches and indigenous movements such as Watchman Nee's 'Little Flock' and the True Jesus Church.
eras/modern-era/globalNotes/2/text: Japan's 'hidden Christians' revealed themselves to French priests in Nagasaki (1865); the Pyongyang Great Revival (1907) shaped Korean Protestantism.
eras/modern-era/globalNotes/3/text: The Bolshevik revolution brought systematic persecution: thousands of clergy were killed, churches closed, and Patriarch Tikhon imprisoned; Stalin partially relaxed restrictions in 1943 for wartime purposes.
eras/modern-era/globalNotes/4/text: The Armenian Genocide (1915–1923), along with massacres of Assyrian and Greek Christians in the Ottoman Empire, destroyed ancient Christian communities of Anatolia and northern Mesopotamia.
eras/modern-era/globalNotes/5/text: Dalit mass movements brought large numbers into Protestant churches; the Malankara church divided between Orthodox and Syriac (Jacobite) factions, and Sadhu Sundar Singh popularised an Indian Christian spirituality.
eras/modern-era/globalNotes/6/text: Liberal governments curtailed church privileges; Mexico's anticlerical laws provoked the Cristero War (1926–1929), while Protestant and early Pentecostal missions (e.g. Chile's Methodist Pentecostal Church, 1910) began to grow.
eras/contemporary/summary: Since 1945 Christianity's centre of gravity has shifted decisively to the Global South, with explosive growth in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America and parts of Asia, while church attendance declined across much of Europe and North America. The Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) transformed Catholic worship and ecumenical relations, the World Council of Churches (1948) and dialogues such as the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999) narrowed old divisions, and Pentecostal-charismatic Christianity became a global force. Christians lived under communism in Eastern Europe and China, faced conflict and emigration in the Middle East, and confronted new questions of liberation, gender, sexuality and abuse.
eras/contemporary/globalNotes/0/text: Christians in sub-Saharan Africa grew from roughly 9% of the population in 1910 to over 60% by 2010, and the region now has the largest Christian population of any continent; leaders such as Desmond Tutu opposed apartheid.
eras/contemporary/globalNotes/1/text: In China, Protestant churches were forced into the Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954) and all churches closed during the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976), yet unregistered house churches multiplied; South Korea became a major missionary-sending nation.
eras/contemporary/globalNotes/2/text: The bishops' conference at Medellín (1968) embraced a 'preferential option for the poor' and liberation theology; Archbishop Óscar Romero was assassinated (1980). Pentecostalism grew rapidly, and in 2013 the Argentine Jorge Bergoglio became Pope Francis.
eras/contemporary/globalNotes/3/text: After Soviet persecution peaked under Khrushchev, the fall of communism (1991) brought an Orthodox revival in Russia and Eastern Europe; the 2018 Moscow–Constantinople rupture over Ukrainian autocephaly divided world Orthodoxy.
eras/contemporary/globalNotes/4/text: War in Lebanon, Iraq and Syria and the rise of ISIS (2014) caused mass emigration of ancient Christian communities from the Middle East; Coptic Christians in Egypt have faced repeated attacks.
eras/contemporary/globalNotes/5/text: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church received its own patriarch (1959) after centuries under Coptic metropolitans; Eritrea's church became autocephalous (1993–1998), and Ethiopian Pentecostal (P'ent'ay) churches grew rapidly.
eras/contemporary/globalNotes/6/text: The Church of South India (1947) united Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches; Christian communities in north-east India (Nagaland, Mizoram) became majority Christian.
